Curiosity is one of our most underrated sources of inspiration. It’s that spark we catch as children when an unfamiliar noise in the house turns into a grand investigation, or when a speck on a leaf prompts us to wonder if there's a whole universe of life hidden in plain sight. As we grow older, life can become routine, and we sometimes forget the value of those small everyday mysteries. Yet, curiosity remains an engine for creativity and delight if we recognize it for what it is: the desire to learn and discover.

In moments of pure curiosity, there’s no immediate agenda—no pressure to be “right” or prove a point. It’s just the joy of exploring something new. Perhaps that’s why it’s such a powerful tool. When you’re truly curious, you set aside preconceived notions and open yourself to what’s unknown. In this mindset, questions become exciting invitations to find something you didn’t know, whether you’re reading a history book, tinkering with a new technology, or exploring a new hobby.

Interestingly, curiosity is often spurred by the smallest experiences. It might be the texture of a certain type of paper, the way sunlight glints off a window at a certain angle, or the pattern of stepping stones in a garden. By leaning into these moments, we can find deep wells of inspiration and creativity. Artists, scientists, and thinkers of all kinds often credit their greatest achievements to that initial curiosity that propelled them forward, whether it was Einstein wondering why the sky is blue or a child playing with building blocks that eventually led them to become an architect.

Wondrous things happen when we approach the world with the mindset of a curious beginner. Self-imposed limitations begin to lift—“can I do this?” transforms into “I’ll at least see what happens,” and that sense of exploration itself becomes immensely rewarding, even if it doesn’t immediately lead to a big revelation.

If you want to nurture curiosity, a good method is simply to pause and ask a question. Simple as it sounds, it helps: “Why is that happening?” “How does this work?” “Could it have been done differently?” In many ways, the best place to start is in your own immediate environment. There’s plenty of mystery in the everyday—your phone’s technology, the way local trees change over the course of a season, or your grandmother’s recipe for a dish passed down through generations. Delving into any one of these mysteries can open up a new world.

Another way to amplify curiosity is to let yourself follow the natural meanderings of your mind, without quickly dismissing an idea as “silly” or “unimportant.” Give yourself permission to go down rabbit holes. Read that article about a medieval castle, then discover the adjacent topic of ancient siege engines, and before you know it, you’re fascinated by the engineering feats of societies centuries before your time. Such explorations reveal unexpected connections: that interest in siege engines might spark insights into structural design, which in turn could inspire a modern-day invention or design pattern.

Life throws a mix of the predictable and the unexpected our way. Cultivating a curious mindset helps us navigate and appreciate both. When things go according to plan, curiosity invites us to dig deeper, refine our understanding, and question how we can make the routine better. When faced with the unpredictable, curiosity reminds us to stand in awe of the unknown, to assess it without fear, and possibly find solutions and perspectives we wouldn’t have uncovered otherwise.

So, in a world that can often feel frenetic or overly structured, treasure your curiosity. Seek out new pieces of information not because you have to impress anyone, but because learning in itself is a source of joy. Start small. Notice a detail you’ve never focused on before. Ask a question. Follow your natural sense of wonder. In doing so, you might rekindle that feeling you knew as a child—of the world crackling with hidden secrets just waiting to be discovered.
